en: Looking at the opposite side -
Munaryktap Kara-Tal.
Between these two
Are many kinds of unseen creatures.
There is a deer, there is a tiger,
Wherever one turns are countless wonders.
Rich in crops, spacious for cattle,
It has countless splendid places.
There are ibex on its terraces,
Argali on its hills,
There's a deer on the bend,
Marshes in patch after patch,
And separate swans and geese.
There is a forest, there is a willow,
Along this Issyk-Köl
Every living creature is found.
It has demoiselle cranes, ducks, and geese,
And many kinds of marshland.
There is a fox on the plain,
For those who dwell there, Issyk-Köl
Has wealth waiting to be found.
Its deep ravines hold many foxes,
And its abundance brings much laughter.
Its thousand valleys are each distinct;
Its delights are famed among the people.
Gold seems poured among its stones,
And the Kyrgyz would settle there content;
Almighty Allah
Made every kind of land.
Could it be a land too small
To pitch a royal camp and hold games?
Could it be a land where one would not shoot
The maral in its marshes?!
O yawning gorge,
Uncle Bakai, O gray wolf,
I have many laments to tell!
The spring flows,
The nightingale sang in wonder,
The listener is moved to tears;
Such an interesting place!
Uncle Bakai, bringer of good fortune,
Look at the forest!
It has noisy wild beasts;
Look at the mountain side
There is snow upon its summit!
Your Almighty God
Truly created this land
In surpassing beauty!
It is a lake that opens one's grief,
It is a place that dispels sorrow.
There are different grasses,
It has lands unlike any others.
My uncle Bakai, my old one,
My beloved saint!
While your gray wolf was alive,
While the wide world remained whole,
While your worthy one was alive,
While your fortune remained whole,
There was no people you had not fought,
No land you had not subdued.
When you humiliated Kokon,
When you alone brought turmoil
Upon the face of the earth,
While your bloodthirsty hero lived,
Kara-Shaar, Kambyl
When you besieged them,
When you beat down
The kalday and the Soloons,
When you caused true upheaval,
When you seized the khanate
When you seized the khanate,
Why didn't you know this place?!
Why, uncle,
Did you not travel through this place?!
Uncle Bakai, my gray wolf,
You failed to see this land—
What a cause for regret!
The world's delight,
A paradise* unseen around the bend,
Has remained here!
Could it be a land where people
Would scatter through the valley and not camp?
Could it be a land where every man
Would not become a hero!
Could it be a land where old women
Would not slice and chew rump-fat?
Could it be a land where brave men
Would not drive a thousand horses?
Could it be a land where men would not strut
In pairs of sable caps!
Could our people camp in neighboring corrals
And fail to prosper!"
Aryslan Bakay started the journey,
At Kongur-Ölöng and Kopo,
He had a sheep slaughtered there;
A gentle breeze, a cool summer,
He pitched the wide screen,
And removed the saddles
From all the fine thoroughbreds.
He rested the coursers overnight,
Keeping them tethered until dawn.
Using Akkangky as a pillow,
All the valiant men
Lay with their heads toward the qibla,*
Resting upon their elbows,
And took a brief sleep.
Not much time had passed
When true dawn arrived
And daybreak turned yellow.
The rim of dawn swelled;
When the cold wind blows,
The boys awoke from sleep.
They let all the fine coursers
Drink their fill of water,
And graze great mouthfuls
Of one fescue among eighty grasses.
From a gushing, pure spring,
Without letting the coursers rise,
They quenched their thirst.
Leading them about for a long while,
They filled the stomachs
Of the fourteen thoroughbred horses with grass.
When the sun reached midmorning,
The companions stood
Serving their prince;
All were champions bound for China.
Such was the condition of the boys.
They loaded the baggage and bustled about,
Bounding and bunching like roe deer,
Drawing the ropes and loading the packs;
Before one could say this or that,
In the blink of an eye,
They loaded the ammunition stored in saddlebags,
Loaded up a great wealth of goods,
And for aged Lord Bakai
Carved rump meat and served him mane-fat,
Dipped bread in fat and gave it to him.
Lion Bakai and Semetey,
With the two companions who followed them,
Set out and traveled on their journey,
Riding hard and covering much ground.
When the sun was sinking low,
At the dark pass of Kapka-Tash,
They halted at Kapka-Tash.
When they stopped, hero Bakai
Lamented his grief from long ago!
His white beard had grown sparse,
And the tears flowing from his two eyes
Poured down over his chest:
“When my noble Manas was alive,
We wore the flanks of our horses lean,
Roaming the four corners
Of the encircling world,
While my lord was alive.
In Beijing of the Kakanchin,
My lord Almam, the leopard, was there;
When I reconnoitered his road,
From its nobles and its khan,
From the great city of Beijing,
When we rode out to reconnoiter the road,
When we went to demand an answer,
Indeed, Almam and I
Stayed at Issyk-Köl.
When we faced and besieged
Beijing, which lay tightly shut,
We lived in this world
Free by our own will for a time.
Almam the formidable and I
Stayed in this very place.
At that time dusk came and the sun set;
The spur of that mountain over there,
The nose of the gray ridge,
Was a slope with a spring.
The shrine that the leopard Almam named
Was called Boz-Uchuk Shrine!
On that broad slope itself
The people pitched their camp;
The gray hill on this side
Was the place where your uncle,
Hero Bakai, kept watch.
My land remains, but my people are gone.
Now that my beard is white,
Now that my journey nears its end,
Parted from those valiant men,
I alone remain alive in this filthy world.
I have none of my own age, none my equal,
No hero to ride beside me!
My dear children,
This was a place where a holy father lay;
They called it Boz-Uchuk-Ata.
Boz-Uchuk is a noble shrine—
Let us camp at Boz-Uchuk!
Let us survey the lay of the land;
O calamity-stricken orphans,
Let us gauge the length of the road!
Clearing enemies and traveling the road,
Let us scout that Beijing!
Let us reach the khan of the Kakanchin,
The teeming city of Beijing,
Measuring the land as we go.
It has nobles, it has giants,
It has peoples of many kinds;
And among those people
There is the blue-mottled, gray-bearded great Manchu,
Hero Kongurbai, famed and mighty.
That raging, death-dealing swine
Has, as you should know, such great renown!
Store an old man’s words in your pack;
Children, listen without making me cry out!
I received it from the transmitters of tradition;
I, your uncle, great Bakai,
Asked those who knew!
Yesterday, in the campaign where giants perished,
In the ordeal my noble lord brought upon them,
There were mighty men and lions,
And there was my champion Almam,
Who could read the Chinese tongue!
When they wreaked slaughter among the Chinese,
The Chinese Shypchaidar and
Giant Tiken—
When the leopard Manas, that bloodthirsty lion,
Seized them and ripped their bellies open,
The fiercest of the Chinese,
Kyrym of the red spear—
That strongman Kyrym
Was knocked from his gray mule,
Struck down by my dear elder brother,
And brave Syrgak of Khan Ulak
Cut off his head.
Deprived of his father,
Kyrym’s son Muradyl
Was left behind at that time,
An orphan while still young.
Living as an orphan, he grew to manhood,
Joined the people of the land,
And, I heard, emerged as a formidable man.
The Kara-Kalmak and the Manchus
Were struck with fear, I heard!
Muradyl learned surpassingly well
The sixty burku and the ilin,
And became learned, I heard!
Against those who had suffered humiliation,
He became an adversary, I heard;
Muradyl could bring down rain
And became a weather-maker, I heard!
Across the face of the sloping land,
At the edge where the enemy descends,
He prepared weapons and took up a spear,
And his face too turned wrathful;
He girded on a sword without a sheath,
And like a cloud about to rain again,
His face turned wrathful.
“If I reach the Burut whose homes burned,
I will wreak slaughter;
I will go and avenge
My father, who died,” he said.
